thread.title: Singapore Launches FirstDate Matchmaking Service for Government Employees Aged 21 to 35
thread.title_full: Singapore Launches FirstDate Matchmaking Service for Government Employees Aged 21 to 35

author: BreitbartNews
title: Singapore Launches FirstDate Matchmaking Service for Government Employees Aged 21 to 35
text:
Singapore launched FirstDate, a matchmaking service for government employees aged 21 to 35, using the Gale-Shapley algorithm to address a 60-year-low birth rate in 2025.
Singapore this week launched FirstDate, a government matchmaking service for public employees aged 21 to 35, designed to help them find a romantic partner. The initiative responds to a national birth rate that fell to a 60-year low in 2025. FirstDate uses the Gale-Shapley Stable Matching Algorithm and matches each user with only one potential partner at a time, offering what the government calls a different approach to dating.
The Gale-Shapley algorithm is not an exciting new discovery that has never been tried before. It was developed in the 1960s and eventually helped to win a Nobel Prize in Economics for co-creator Lloyd Shapley in 2012. It has been used in many earlier dating services, and also for non-romantic matching tasks such as matching university applicants to the most ideal schools. The system is sometimes called the Stable Marriage Algorithm because matching men and women into lasting marriages was a metaphor for the statistical problem it was designed to solve.
The algorithm works by matching people in rounds and then giving the matched participants other offers to consider, until everyone has a match they prefer to all other possible matches. The algorithm is not infallible, which led some critics of the FirstDate program to think the government was making unrealistic promises to help all of its employees find a permanent marriage partner. Others complained that it was unfair to limit the service to only government employees, or criticized the narrow age range of participants as obvious evidence that FirstDate is more like a breeding program than a dating service. Some social media users denounced it as dystopian in character.
An optimistic young employee of the Singaporean defense ministry said the experience of meeting someone through an application does not change much across the applications. But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower, the employee added, because we are all public servants looking for a partner. A less optimistic commentator on social media grumbled that the government is only doing this to raise the total fertility rate and does not actually care about whether users find a partner otherwise.
The BBC noted Singapore has a long history of concocting government programs to stave off demographic decline, including government-organized social mixers and agencies to promote marriage. FirstDate was created during an annual hackathon sponsored by Singapore's technology agency, which was tasked with creating a system that would avoid the swipe right fatigue afflicting clients of casual dating sites. Instead of casting singles adrift in a turbulent sea of potential mates, FirstDate is supposed to steer people toward compatible matches and then suggest activities they can participate in.
An early version of the program offered a government-subsidized first date meal to each couple. The current version will not offer any other matches to a couple until they either reject each other or have a first date, at which point they become invisible to all other users.
Singapore Management University psychology professor Norman Li explained that limiting the choice set resets the dating environment to one that is more manageable by human brains. The imprimatur of a government service was considered important because Singaporeans are comfortable with computers but particularly vulnerable to scams.
Like other Asian countries, and indeed many developed nations around the world, Singapore is grappling with low fertility rates and an aging population, and like other countries it has discovered that merely offering subsidies for childbirth is not enough to reverse the decline. In 2025, Singapore's total fertility rate fell to 0.87 births per woman, from 0.97 in 2024 and well below the population replacement rate of 2.1.
